Decision: Selected customer segmentation as the primary lens
Options_Considered: Customer segmentation; product association; customer value and retention
Selected_Option: Customer segmentation
Reason: The transaction data supports customer-level behavioural profiling through engineered purchasing features
Evidence: The dataset contains CustomerID, InvoiceDate, Quantity, and UnitPrice variables
Impact: Defines the main unit of analysis and modeling strategy

Decision: Selected product association and bundling as the secondary lens
Options_Considered: No secondary lens; overall association mining; segment-specific association mining
Selected_Option: Segment-specific product association and bundling
Reason: This directly strengthens the primary lens by producing product recommendations for suitable customer segments
Evidence: InvoiceNo and StockCode support basket construction while CustomerID connects baskets to customer segments
Impact: Adds coherent cross-selling and bundling recommendations

Decision: Excluded the raw Excel dataset from Git tracking
Options_Considered: Commit raw data to GitHub; store externally and document access
Selected_Option: Store externally and document the source, path, and fingerprint
Reason: The dataset is publicly available and approximately 23 MB; excluding it keeps the repository lightweight while preserving reproducibility
Evidence: The UCI dataset page, DOI, local path, and SHA-256 fingerprint are documented
Impact: Every member must download and verify the same dataset file

Decision: Adopted a fixed random seed
Options_Considered: Use unspecified seeds; use different seeds; use one documented seed
Selected_Option: Use random_state=42 where applicable
Reason: A fixed seed makes model fitting, sampling, and initial validation results reproducible
Evidence: The same seed can be reused across notebooks and verified by all members
Impact: Improves repeatability while stability will still be assessed using additional seeds

Decision: Investigated exact duplicate rows before preprocessing
Options_Considered: Retain all rows; remove every repeated InvoiceNo; retain one copy of exact duplicate records
Selected_Option: Retain one copy of each exact duplicate record
Reason: Repeated InvoiceNo values are legitimate because invoices contain multiple product lines, but exact repetition across all eight fields may inflate analytical measures
Evidence: 5268 additional exact duplicate rows were identified across 4879 duplicate groups
Impact: Exact duplicates will be removed during preprocessing while the raw dataset remains unchanged

Decision: Defined preliminary purchase-validity conditions
Options_Considered: Include all transactions; exclude only C-prefixed invoices; require non-cancellation invoices with positive Quantity and UnitPrice
Selected_Option: Require non-cancellation InvoiceNo, Quantity greater than zero, and UnitPrice greater than zero
Reason: Cancellations, returns, stock adjustments, and non-positive prices can distort purchase revenue and RFM measures
Evidence: 9288 cancellation rows, 10624 negative-quantity rows, and 2517 non-positive-price rows were identified
Impact: Creates a valid purchase-only source while retaining excluded records separately for investigation

Decision: Defined CustomerID handling by analytical task
Options_Considered: Impute missing IDs; treat each missing row as a customer; exclude missing IDs from customer-level analysis
Selected_Option: Exclude missing CustomerID rows from customer segmentation and segment-specific rules
Reason: Missing customer identifiers cannot be reliably reconstructed or assigned to a customer
Evidence: 135080 rows have missing CustomerID, representing 24.93 percent of the raw data
Impact: Customer segmentation coverage is reduced, but invalid customer attribution and fabricated identities are avoided

Decision: Selected StockCode as the product identifier
Options_Considered: Use Description; use StockCode; combine StockCode and Description as separate products
Selected_Option: Use StockCode with a canonical description for reporting
Reason: StockCode is the stable item identifier while descriptions contain spelling and naming variations
Evidence: 217 StockCodes have multiple cleaned descriptions
Impact: Prevents the same product from being split into several items during association mining

Decision: Defined preliminary handling of administrative StockCodes
Options_Considered: Treat all codes as merchandise; remove every code without digits; use an explicit reviewed administrative-code list
Selected_Option: Use an explicit reviewed administrative-code list
Reason: Some letter-only codes are genuine merchandise while other codes represent fees, postage, samples, or adjustments
Evidence: 2310 candidate administrative rows worth GBP 394205.67 were identified; DCGSSBOY and DCGSSGIRL are genuine products
Impact: Administrative codes will be excluded from product association rules and tested through monetary-feature sensitivity analysis

Decision: Avoided automatic outlier deletion
Options_Considered: Remove all IQR outliers; cap automatically; investigate and compare transformations
Selected_Option: Retain extreme observations for investigation and perform transformation and sensitivity analysis
Reason: Large observations may represent genuine wholesale customers rather than errors
Evidence: Maximum valid line quantity is 80995 and maximum valid line value is GBP 168469.60; top 1 percent of customers generate 32.20 percent of revenue
Impact: Prevents unjustified information loss while requiring log transformation, robust scaling, and stability checks

Decision: Flagged the final month as incomplete
Options_Considered: Treat every month equally; remove December 2011; retain and explicitly flag the partial month
Selected_Option: Retain December 2011 and flag it as partial
Reason: The dataset ends on 09 December 2011, so the final month cannot be compared directly with complete monthly totals
Evidence: December 2011 contains records only from 01 to 09 December
Impact: Recency calculations can use the latest date, but seasonality conclusions must identify the incomplete month

Decision: Recognised geographic imbalance in the analysis
Options_Considered: Restrict immediately to UK; encode Country in clustering; retain all countries and conduct sensitivity analysis
Selected_Option: Retain all countries initially and consider a UK-only sensitivity analysis
Reason: The full dataset provides broader coverage, but the dominant UK market could control cluster patterns
Evidence: The UK represents 91.45 percent of valid purchase rows and 84.59 percent of valid purchase revenue
Impact: Country will not automatically be used as a distance feature; geographic limitations and sensitivity results will be reported

Decision: Created separate task-specific processed datasets
Options_Considered: Create one universal cleaned dataset; create separate datasets for segmentation association rules returns and administrative records
Selected_Option: Create separate task-specific datasets
Reason: Customer segmentation and association mining require different units of analysis and eligibility conditions
Evidence: Final outputs contain 391150 customer-merchandise rows 522568 basket rows 10587 return-adjustment rows and 2310 administrative rows
Impact: Prevents one cleaning rule from incorrectly removing information required by another task

Decision: Standardised identifier and text fields
Options_Considered: Retain imported types; convert identifiers to numeric measures; standardise identifiers as categorical values
Selected_Option: Standardise text fields and convert identified CustomerID values to integer identifiers
Reason: InvoiceNo StockCode and CustomerID are identifiers rather than continuous measurements; consistent formatting prevents grouping errors
Evidence: Standardisation created zero additional duplicate records and valid purchase descriptions contained zero missing values
Impact: Produces consistent invoice product and customer grouping keys for downstream analysis

Decision: Created LineTotal after purchase validation
Options_Considered: Use raw Quantity multiplied by UnitPrice; calculate after filtering; omit transaction value
Selected_Option: Calculate LineTotal as positive Quantity multiplied by positive UnitPrice after purchase-validity filtering
Reason: Calculating after validation prevents cancellations returns and invalid prices from being treated as positive purchase revenue
Evidence: All 391150 primary customer merchandise rows have positive Quantity UnitPrice and LineTotal
Impact: Provides a valid monetary measure for RFM and customer-value features

Decision: Excluded generated processed datasets from Git and recorded fingerprints
Options_Considered: Commit large processed CSV files; exclude them without evidence; regenerate locally and record fingerprints
Selected_Option: Regenerate processed datasets locally and document row counts file sizes and SHA-256 fingerprints
Reason: Processed datasets are reproducible from the verified raw file and executable preprocessing notebook while Git remains lightweight
Evidence: All four processed files passed reload validation and their SHA-256 fingerprints were saved
Impact: Each member can reproduce and verify identical processed outputs before downstream analysis

Decision: Adopted a fixed customer-analysis date
Options_Considered: Use system date; use latest transaction date; use one day after latest transaction
Selected_Option: Use 2011-12-10, one day after the latest transaction
Reason: A fixed analysis date produces reproducible recency values while keeping all customers at least one day from the reference date
Evidence: The latest purchase transaction occurred on 2011-12-09
Impact: Makes Recency reproducible across all notebooks and team members

Decision: Defined Frequency using distinct purchase invoices
Options_Considered: Count transaction rows; count products; count distinct invoices
Selected_Option: Count distinct InvoiceNo values per customer
Reason: Transaction rows represent individual product lines while invoices represent separate purchasing occasions
Evidence: The customer merchandise dataset contains 391150 rows but only 18402 distinct invoices
Impact: Produces a meaningful customer purchase-frequency measure

Decision: Selected RFM as the core clustering feature set
Options_Considered: RFM; quantity-based features; all engineered features
Selected_Option: Recency, Frequency, and Monetary
Reason: RFM provides an established and interpretable representation of customer purchasing behaviour
Evidence: All 4334 customers have complete Recency, Frequency, and Monetary values
Impact: Provides the primary baseline input for customer segmentation

Decision: Selected an enhanced candidate feature set
Options_Considered: Core RFM only; all engineered variables; RFM with behavioural diversity variables
Selected_Option: Recency, Frequency, Monetary, ProductDiversity, and AverageBasketSize
Reason: Product diversity and average basket size add behavioural information without directly duplicating total spending and quantity
Evidence: Correlation analysis showed strong redundancy between Monetary and TotalQuantity while the selected behavioural variables provide complementary information
Impact: Enables comparison between a simple RFM model and a richer behavioural model

Decision: Excluded redundant and incomplete variables from direct clustering input
Options_Considered: Include all engineered variables; delete them; retain them for profiling
Selected_Option: Retain TotalQuantity, AverageOrderValue, TenureDays, AverageDaysBetweenPurchases, and TransactionRows for profiling and diagnostics
Reason: TotalQuantity strongly correlates with Monetary; TenureDays strongly relates to Frequency; purchase intervals are unavailable for one-purchase customers
Evidence: Pearson correlation between Monetary and TotalQuantity was 0.92; Spearman correlation between Frequency and TenureDays was 0.90; 1505 customers have no purchase interval
Impact: Reduces duplicated weighting and avoids unnecessary imputation while preserving variables for interpretation

Decision: Applied log1p transformation to skewed clustering features
Options_Considered: Use raw values; delete extreme customers; winsorise values; apply log1p transformation
Selected_Option: Create both raw and log1p feature datasets
Reason: Customer purchase features are strongly right-skewed and log1p reduces the influence of extreme legitimate customers without deleting them
Evidence: Monetary skewness reduced from 19.58 to 0.40 and ProductDiversity from 6.92 to -0.24
Impact: Supports fair raw-versus-transformed model comparison during clustering

Decision: Deferred feature scaling to the clustering stage
Options_Considered: Scale during feature engineering; store only scaled data; scale within each clustering experiment
Selected_Option: Preserve raw and log-transformed values and apply scaling within model pipelines
Reason: Different clustering algorithms and experiments may require different scaling methods
Evidence: Both core and enhanced raw and log datasets were saved and passed reload validation
Impact: Prevents premature commitment to one scaler and avoids information loss

Decision: Used merchandise-only monetary value as the primary customer measure
Options_Considered: Include all administrative charges; exclude administrative rows; replace merchandise monetary value
Selected_Option: Use merchandise-only Monetary and retain an administrative-value sensitivity dataset
Reason: Administrative charges do not directly represent product purchasing behaviour although they may affect customer value
Evidence: 541 primary customers had administrative value; median affected-customer monetary change was 9.42 percent while the overall customer rank correlation remained approximately 1.00
Impact: Keeps customer segmentation product-focused while documenting sensitivity to administrative charges

Decision: Created an interpretable RFM baseline
Options_Considered: No baseline; manual customer labels; quartile-based RFM scoring
Selected_Option: Quartile-based RFM scoring baseline
Reason: A transparent baseline is required to compare and interpret unsupervised clustering results
Evidence: All 4334 customers received Recency, Frequency and Monetary scores from 1 to 4
Impact: Provides an explainable benchmark for data-driven segmentation

Decision: Compared raw and transformed feature representations with two scalers
Options_Considered: Use one feature representation; compare raw and log data; compare one or multiple scalers
Selected_Option: Evaluate core and enhanced raw/log feature sets with StandardScaler and RobustScaler
Reason: Clustering results can be sensitive to skewness, feature selection and scaling
Evidence: Eight preprocessing configurations and 72 K-Means experiments were evaluated
Impact: Provides evidence-based preprocessing and model selection

Decision: Rejected misleading raw-feature clustering solutions
Options_Considered: Select the highest silhouette model; automatically delete extreme customers; apply practical balance screening
Selected_Option: Retain all customers and reject solutions with operationally unusable cluster imbalance
Reason: Raw-feature solutions achieved high silhouette scores by isolating very small groups of extreme customers
Evidence: The highest-scoring raw solution placed 99.82 percent of customers in one cluster
Impact: Prevents selection of a statistically attractive but commercially unusable model

Decision: Compared multiple clustering algorithms
Options_Considered: Use K-Means only; compare K-Means and one alternative; compare multiple distinct algorithms
Selected_Option: Compare K-Means, Agglomerative Clustering, Gaussian Mixture Models and DBSCAN
Reason: Different algorithms make different assumptions about cluster geometry and density
Evidence: A total of 192 unique clustering experiments were evaluated
Impact: Strengthens model comparison and assignment evidence

Decision: Used multiple internal evaluation metrics and practical balance criteria
Options_Considered: Use silhouette only; use one alternative metric; combine metrics and operational criteria
Selected_Option: Use Silhouette, Davies-Bouldin, Calinski-Harabasz, cluster size and noise percentage
Reason: No single internal metric fully captures cluster quality or business usability
Evidence: Raw models with high silhouette scores showed extreme cluster imbalance
Impact: Supports a more defensible model-selection process

Decision: Evaluated clustering stability
Options_Considered: Use one fixed fit only; test random seeds; test seeds and customer resampling
Selected_Option: Use ten random seeds and thirty repeated 80 percent customer samples
Reason: Stable segments should not change substantially because of initialization or moderate sample variation
Evidence: The selected model achieved mean seed ARI of approximately 0.99 and mean resampling ARI of approximately 0.93
Impact: Provides evidence that final customer assignments are reproducible and robust

Decision: Selected a five-cluster K-Means solution
Options_Considered: Select k=3 using highest silhouette; select k=4 as a compromise; select k=5 for actionable detail
Selected_Option: K-Means with five clusters using log-transformed core RFM features and StandardScaler
Reason: The five-cluster model preserved competitive metrics and stability while producing more actionable profiles for segment-specific association mining
Evidence: Silhouette was approximately 0.32, Davies-Bouldin approximately 0.98, cluster sizes ranged from 8.26 to 26.21 percent, and resampling mean ARI was approximately 0.93
Impact: Defines the final customer segmentation used by downstream analysis

Decision: Assigned business-readable names to final clusters
Options_Considered: Retain numeric cluster labels; assign labels automatically; assign names after original-scale profiling
Selected_Option: Name clusters Hibernating Low Value, Recent Low Engagement, At Risk Regular, Loyal High Value and Champions
Reason: Numeric cluster identifiers are arbitrary and do not communicate customer behaviour
Evidence: Original-scale Recency, Frequency, Monetary and behavioural profiles showed five distinct customer groups
Impact: Improves interpretation and supports targeted recommendations

Decision: Prepared segment assignments for association mining
Options_Considered: Provide only model metrics; provide cluster labels without customer identifiers; provide validated customer-level assignments
Selected_Option: Save validated CustomerID, cluster and segment assignments with fingerprints
Reason: Segment-specific basket mining requires a reliable connection between customers and their assigned segments
Evidence: All 4334 customers received one unique assignment across five segments and reload validation passed
Impact: Enables Senaratne P.A.R.T. to perform segment-specific association mining

Decision: Performed association mining separately for each customer segment
Options_Considered: Mine all transactions together; analyse segments descriptively only; mine separate baskets for each segment
Selected_Option: Use segment-specific invoice-product baskets
Reason: Different customer groups may demonstrate different purchasing relationships that an overall model can conceal
Evidence: 391150 transaction rows and 18402 invoices were linked to 4334 customers across five validated segments
Impact: Enables targeted cross-selling and bundle recommendations for each customer segment

Decision: Selected FP-Growth with adaptive support and interpretable itemset limits
Options_Considered: Apriori; FP-Growth with one global threshold; FP-Growth with segment-adaptive support
Selected_Option: FP-Growth with support equal to the maximum of 1 percent or 20 segment invoices and maximum itemset length three
Reason: FP-Growth efficiently processes sparse baskets while adaptive support accounts for different segment invoice volumes
Evidence: Five sparse baskets contained 1364 to 7183 invoices with densities below 0.72 percent
Impact: Produces computationally feasible and interpretable segment-level frequent itemsets

Decision: Applied multi-metric practical rule filtering and ranking
Options_Considered: Rank by confidence only; rank by lift only; combine support, confidence, lift and leverage
Selected_Option: Require at least 25 supporting invoices, 40 percent confidence, lift of 1.50 and positive leverage, followed by balanced percentile ranking
Reason: Confidence alone can favour popular consequents and lift alone can favour rare relationships
Evidence: 2361 practical rules passed the combined quality criteria across five segments
Impact: Reduces weak or misleading rules and prioritises commercially useful patterns

Decision: Evaluated association-rule sensitivity to minimum-support selection
Options_Considered: Use one threshold without validation; compare two thresholds; compare four support thresholds
Selected_Option: Compare support thresholds of 0.008, 0.010, 0.0125 and 0.015
Reason: Rule discoveries should be assessed for dependence on parameter selection
Evidence: Twenty sensitivity experiments showed that lower support substantially increased rule volume while stricter thresholds retained approximately 24 to 54 percent of baseline rules
Impact: Supports 1 percent as a balanced baseline for coverage and reliability

Decision: Converted association rules into diverse segment-specific recommendations
Options_Considered: Report every valid rule; select rules only by lift; select balanced recommendations with unique consequent products
Selected_Option: Select eight high-quality recommendations with distinct consequent products for each segment
Reason: A concise and diverse rule set is easier to translate into marketing and cross-selling actions
Evidence: Forty final recommendations were produced, eight for each of five customer segments
Impact: Provides actionable product recommendations for reactivation, retention, loyalty and VIP campaigns
